title: Your foot never falls asleep. Here's what does 🦶
description:
Why does your foot 'fall asleep'? It isn't the blood: neurologists say it's a squashed nerve. Cross your legs and the common fibular (peroneal) nerve, which wraps around the bone just below the outside of your knee, close to the skin, gets pressed. Like a kinked hose, its signals between brain and foot stop, so the foot goes numb and floppy. When you move, the nerve wakes up and the tingling, pins and needles (paresthesia), is it coming back online. That annoying buzz makes you shift before a long squeeze can injure the nerve. (How the body works, not medical advice.)

Sources: The Conversation (What happens when your foot falls asleep); ScienceAlert (neurologists Rebecca Traub and Steven Vernino); Colorado Orthopedics (peroneal nerve palsy); Penn Medicine (common peroneal nerve dysfunction).

claims.claim: a foot 'falls asleep' because a nerve is compressed; lack of blood flow is a common misconception
the common fibular (peroneal) nerve wraps around the fibular head below the outside of the knee, close to the skin; crossing the legs compresses it
compression blocks the nerve's signals like a kinked hose: numbness and trouble moving
pins and needles (paresthesia) happen as the nerve regains function
the discomfort makes you shift position; prolonged compression (e.g. someone who can't move) can injure a nerve
